title: Aesthetic judgment of architecture for Chinese observers
research_question: To investigate whether the preference for contours, ceiling height, and openness, previously observed in Western cultures, also exists among Chinese observers.

participants.description: College students (19 males, 10 females; mean age 23.05±1.99 years for males, 23.00±2.00 years for females), right-handed, no visual impairments or color blindness, normal or corrected vision, and no history of psychosis or neuropathy. From Zhejiang University School of Medicine.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: 200 real photos of architectural interior spaces, categorized by 3 factors (ceiling height, openness, contour) each with 2 levels (high/low ceiling, open/closed space, curvilinear/rectilinear contours). This created 8 conditions of 25 pictures each.

measures.instrument: 5-point Likert scale (1 = very unpleasant, 5 = very pleasant)
5-point Likert scale (1 = very ugly, 5 = very beautiful)

findings.antecedent: Architectural space with lower ceilings and less open space (closed)
findings.mechanism: Contour preference is modulated by ceiling height and openness.
findings.quote: For architectural space with lower ceilings and less open space, curvilinear contours were rated higher than rectilinear contours (p<0.05).

findings.antecedent: Architectural space with lower ceilings and more open space
findings.mechanism: Contour preference is modulated by ceiling height and openness.
findings.quote: In the combination of lower ceilings and more open space, rectilinear contours were more likely to lead to a high beauty and pleasantness score (p<0.05).

findings.antecedent: Buildings with lower ceilings and rectilinear contours OR higher ceilings and rectilinear contours OR higher ceilings and curvilinear contours
findings.consequent: Preference for more open space (vs. less open space)
findings.mechanism: Openness preference is modulated by ceiling height and contour type.
findings.quote: When buildings have lower ceilings and rectilinear contours or higher ceilings and rectilinear contours or higher ceilings and curvilinear contours, more open space is more likely to lead to a higher beauty and pleasantness score than is less open space (p<0.05).

findings.antecedent: Among various combinations of openness and contour type
findings.consequent: Preference for higher ceilings (vs. lower ceilings)
findings.mechanism: Ceiling height preference is modulated by openness and contour type.
findings.quote: Among the 4 combinations, compared to lower ceilings, higher ceilings were more likely to lead to a higher beauty and pleasantness score (p<0.05).

mechanisms: Aesthetic judgment is influenced by specific sensory features of architectural space, triggering positive or negative emotional responses.
implementation_implications: Architects should consider the aesthetic experience of potential users when designing architectures.
Designing with high ceilings and open spaces is generally preferred by Chinese observers.
The preference for curvilinear contours is context-dependent, being preferred only when ceilings are low and space is closed.

limitations: The study only employed Chinese observers, limiting the ability to quantify whether architectural feature preferences vary across cultures.
Further studies are needed to test if Western observers also prefer curvilinear contours only when the ceiling is low and the space is enclosed.

paper_metadata.title: Aesthetic judgment of architecture for Chinese observers
paper_metadata.crossref_title: Aesthetic judgment of architecture for Chinese observers
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: Architects should consider the aesthetic experience of potential users when designing architectures. Previous studies have shown that subjective aesthetic judgment of architectures is influenced by structure features, and Western observers prefer structures that have curvilinear contours, high ceilings, and open space. The building styles, however, vary across cultures, and it remains unclear whether the preference for contours, ceiling height, and openness exist across cultures. To investigate this issue, this study analyzes the aesthetic judgment of Chinese observers, and the results demonstrate that Chinese observers also prefer high ceilings and open space. Preference for curvilinear contours, however, interacts with ceiling height and openness. Simple effect analysis reveals that Chinese observers prefer curvilinear contours only when the ceiling is low and the space is closed. In sum, these results suggest that preference for high ceilings and open space is robust for Chinese observers, but the preference for curvilinear contours is less reliable.
